results.title: Create a Safety & Security Framework
results.requirement: Define a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework that conceptually describes how systemic risks are assessed, accepted, and mitigated across the model lifecycle.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define, at a conceptual and descriptive level, the key elements required for systemic risk management under the Safety and Security Chapter (including trigger points, risk acceptance logic, mitigation expectations, responsibility allocation, external input, and update processes)?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly describes its purpose as managing systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models.
The framework outlines how systemic risks are identified, assessed, and mitigated at a high level.
The framework describes trigger points at which additional evaluations or assessments would occur during the model lifecycle.
The framework defines how systemic risk acceptability is determined, including the use of risk tiers or acceptance criteria.
The framework describes, at a high level, expected categories or types of safety and security mitigations associated with different risk levels.
The framework explains how responsibility for systemic risk assessment and mitigation is allocated within the organization.
The framework describes whether and how input from external actors may influence risk-related decisions.
The framework describes how and under what conditions the framework itself would be reviewed or updated.
results.reasoning: Evidence supports indicators 2, 6, 7, and 8 (high-level risk management, responsibility allocation, external input consideration, and update processes). Indicators 3 (trigger points), 4 (risk acceptance tiers), and 5 (mitigations by risk level) are not explicitly defined in the text, and thus cannot be considered satisfied; these operational elements cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle risk management functions (GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE)
Risk tolerance and accountability mechanisms with update/versioning
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit trigger points for additional systemic risk evaluations during the AI lifecycle are not defined.
Formal mechanism for incorporating input from external actors into risk decisions is not established.
Explicit risk acceptance logic, including defined risk tiers or acceptance criteria, is missing.
Explicit mapping of safety and security mitigations to risk levels or tiers is missing.
Explicit criteria or triggers for updating the framework beyond periodic reviews are missing.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Partially; the AI RMF conceptualizes systemic risk management via GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE, including risk tolerance and accountability and update processes, but it does not explicitly define trigger points or how external input directly informs risk decisions.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework provides high-level risk management structure, accountability, and update mechanisms that align with the EU requirement, but it lacks explicit specification of trigger points and explicit handling of external input in risk decisions.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle risk management functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The AI RMF covers governance, lifecycle risk management, accountability, and update/versioning, but it does not define explicit trigger points for re-evaluations, nor does it formalize external input into risk decisions, nor provide a concrete risk-acceptance framework or mitigations-by-risk-level mapping.
missing_elements: Explicit trigger points for additional systemic risk evaluations during the AI lifecycle (e.g., after major model updates, incidents, or changes in threat landscape).
Formal mechanism for incorporating input from external actors into risk decisions (stakeholder engagement protocols, external risk input channels, or governance bodies with external input).
Explicit risk acceptance logic, including defined risk tiers or acceptance criteria (thresholds, decision rights, and escalation rules).
Explicit mapping of safety and security mitigations to risk levels or tiers (which mitigations apply at high, medium, or low risk).
Explicit criteria or triggers for updating the framework beyond periodic reviews (e.g., regulatory changes, significant threat landscape shifts).
weaker_areas: External input influence on risk decisions is mentioned only in general terms and not formalized into the risk decision processes.
scope_divergences: No explicit trigger points for lifecycle re-evaluations (the framework mentions periodic review but does not define lifecycle-embedded triggers).
Lack of a formal external-input integration mechanism into systemic risk decisions (diverges from a requirement to specify how external input informs risk decisions).
No explicit risk-acceptance framework with defined tiers/acceptance criteria (diverges from EU requirement for explicit acceptance logic).
Absence of a clear risk-tiered mitigations catalog (diverges from EU expectation of mitigation categories by risk level).

organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some

AI RMF.

are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and

selected_evidence.text:
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

Framework will employ a two-number versioning system to track and identify major and minor changes. The
first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will
change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number
(e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including
version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook
frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time
and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.

Organizations need to establish and maintain the appropriate accountability mechanisms,

results.title: Implement the Safety & Security Framework
results.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework is intended to be applied across the entire model lifecycle, including continuous systemic risk assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how its systemic risk assessment and mitigation processes are intended to be applied across the model lifecycle, including continuous assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident consideration, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risks are continuously assessed along the entire model lifecycle.
The framework explains how lighter-touch evaluations are conducted at predefined trigger points (e.g. based on time, development stage, compute, access, or affordances).
The framework describes how post-market monitoring is conducted to inform ongoing systemic risk assessment.
The framework explains how information about serious incidents or near misses is taken into account within the risk assessment process.

The framework describes how results from trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, or incident inputs can lead to deeper analysis or escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
The framework outlines the sequence or structure of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).
results.reasoning: Indicator 1 (lifecycle-spanning governance with ongoing monitoring) is present, but indicators 2–5 are not. There is no explicit trigger-point evaluation mechanism, post-market monitoring described as an input to ongoing systemic risk assessment, integration of incident inputs into the risk process with actionable escalation to a full systemic risk assessment, or a defined five-step full systemic risk assessment sequence. The missing operational indicators are not offset by thematic alignment alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle-spanning governance (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Regular/continuous monitoring and improvement
Contingency/incident handling mechanisms
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit trigger-point evaluation mechanism (lighter-touch assessments at predefined trigger points).
Post-market monitoring described as an input to ongoing systemic risk assessment.
Incorporation of information about serious incidents or near misses within the risk assessment process.
Clear escalation pathways to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process when trigger-points or incidents occur.
Defined sequence/structure of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text partially answers the question: it describes lifecycle-spanning governance (GOV/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE) and ongoing monitoring, but omits explicit trigger-point evaluations, incident inputs, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework shows lifecycle-spanning governance and ongoing monitoring, which aligns with continuous risk assessment. It does not fully satisfy the EU requirement due to missing explicit trigger-point evaluations, incident input usage, and escalation pathways to a full systemic risk assessment.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle-spanning governance (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Regular/continuous monitoring and contingency planning

evidence_citations.quote: Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Explicitly states that governance functions cover stages of the AI lifecycle, signaling lifecycle-wide applicability.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework describes how systemic risks are continuously assessed along the entire model lifecycle.

evidence_citations.quote: The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events. After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring and improvement will be in place.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Explicit reference to regular monitoring and ongoing risk management after management activities.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework describes how post-market monitoring is conducted to inform ongoing systemic risk assessment.

evidence_citations.quote: GOV 6.2: Contingency processes are in place to handle failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed to be high-risk.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Shows existence of contingency/incident handling mechanisms relevant to risk assessment, although not detailing their use in escalation.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: The framework describes incident inputs or inputs from incidents and near misses as part of risk processes.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: While lifecycle governance and ongoing monitoring are described, explicit trigger-point evaluations, incident inputs integration, escalation to a full systemic risk assessment, and a defined sequence for such a process are not described.
missing_elements: Explicit trigger-point evaluation mechanism (lighter-touch assessments at predefined trigger points such as time, development stage, compute, access, or affordances).
Post-market monitoring described to inform ongoing systemic risk assessment.
Incorporation of information about serious incidents or near misses within the risk assessment process.
Clear escalation pathways to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process when trigger-points or incidents occur.
Defined sequence/structure of the full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, and re-assessment).
weaker_areas: Ongoing/regular monitoring is referenced, but there is no explicit linkage to a continuous systemic risk assessment across the entire lifecycle or to defined trigger-based escalation.
scope_divergences: No explicit description of a formal, five-step full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process (identification, analysis, acceptability determination, mitigation, re-assessment) as required by EU guidance.
Lack of explicit trigger-point evaluations with concrete criteria and escalation pathways.
Absence of explicit post-market monitoring described as a distinct input to ongoing systemic risk assessment.
Absence of explicit use of incident inputs or near-miss information within the risk assessment process.
No explicit escalation mechanism to initiate a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process based on trigger-points or incident-derived findings.

synthesis_result.justification: Indicator 1 (lifecycle-spanning governance with ongoing monitoring) is present, but indicators 2–5 are not. There is no explicit trigger-point evaluation mechanism, post-market monitoring described as an input to ongoing systemic risk assessment, integration of incident inputs into the risk process with actionable escalation to a full systemic risk assessment, or a defined five-step full systemic risk assessment sequence. The missing operational indicators are not offset by thematic alignment alone.

5.2
Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.

AI RMF 1.0
This complexity and varying levels of visibility can introduce uncertainty into risk management practices. Anticipating, assessing, and otherwise addressing potential sources of
negative risk can mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the integrity of the decision process.

Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.

This complexity and varying levels of visibility can introduce uncertainty into risk management practices. Anticipating, assessing, and otherwise addressing potential sources of
negative risk can mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the integrity of the decision process.

results.title: Framework updates
results.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework defines the conditions, processes, and scope for periodic and event-driven framework assessments and updates, including versioning, changelogs, and remediation planning, in line with Measure 1.3 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define how and when framework assessments and updates are intended to occur, including assessment triggers, periodic review, evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, and the handling of remediation and versioning?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that it is subject to periodic reassessment (e.g. at defined intervals) and to reassessment when specified conditions or events occur.

The framework describes conditions or triggers that would lead to a framework assessment (e.g. material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
The framework explains the scope of a framework assessment, including the evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
The framework explains that framework adherence is assessed, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
The framework describes how findings from a framework assessment may lead to updates of the framework to keep it state-of-the-art.
The framework describes that updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog explaining the nature and rationale of changes.
The framework describes how remediation plans are intended to be defined when framework assessments identify risks of continued or future non-adherence.
results.reasoning: Evidence shows periodic reassessment cadence, versioning with a changelog, and a living-document approach. Missing indicators are explicit event-driven assessment triggers, defined assessment scope/adequacy evaluation, formal adherence assessment, and remediation planning; their absence cannot be offset by periodic updates alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Periodic reassessment at defined intervals (semi-annual)
Versioning with a changelog
Living document with ongoing updates and stakeholder feedback
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit event-driven assessment triggers (conditions or events that would trigger a framework assessment)
Defined scope of a framework assessment, including evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to systemic risks
Formal mechanism for assessing framework adherence, including how non-adherence is identified and its causes
Remediation planning processes to address risks from assessments and how remediation findings lead to updates

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text partially addresses SS-1.3 by detailing periodic assessments/updates, versioning with a changelog, and ongoing ‘living document’ updates, but it does not explicitly define event-driven assessment triggers, the assessment scope, adherence evaluation, or remediation planning.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework establishes periodic review, versioning, and ongoing updates, but it lacks explicit event-triggered assessment triggers, adherence evaluation scope, and remediation planning.
key_aligned_concepts: Periodic reassessment at defined intervals (semi-annual)
Versioning with a changelog
Living document with ongoing updates and stakeholder feedback

Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number (e.g., 1.1). evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates formal versioning and changelog documentation for framework updates.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Indicator: Updates are versioned with a changelog (operational).

evidence_citations.quote: NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Shows a defined cadence for updates to the framework content via semi-annual integration.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Indicator: Periodic reassessment/defined intervals (operational).

evidence_citations.quote: Be a living document. The AI RMF should be readily updated as technology, understanding, and approaches to AI trustworthiness and uses of AI change and as stakeholders learn from implementing AI risk management generally and this framework in particular.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Articulates the expectation that the framework evolves with changing understanding and practice.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Indicator: Updates keep framework state-of-the-art (conceptual/operational).

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The framework covers periodic reassessment and versioning with a living document, but it omits explicit event-driven assessment triggers, explicit assessment scope/adequacy evaluation, adherence assessment, and remediation planning.
missing_elements: Explicit event-driven assessment triggers (conditions or events that would trigger a framework assessment, such as material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, or materially changed systemic risks).
Defined scope of a framework assessment, including explicit evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to systemic risks of the AI models.
Formal mechanism for assessing framework adherence, including how non-adherence is identified and its causes analyzed.
Remediation planning processes to address risks from assessments, including how remediation findings lead to framework updates and responsibilities for remediation actions.
weaker_areas: Adherence evaluation—the text does not define the scope or method for assessing adherence to the framework.
Assessment scope and adequacy evaluation—no explicit description of what the framework assessment should examine beyond periodic updates.
scope_divergences: Lacks explicit event-driven assessment triggers; the EU requirement calls for conditions/events that trigger assessments, not only periodic reviews.
Remediation planning is not described; the EU requirement expects remediation planning when risks of non-adherence are identified.
Explicit evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to systemic risks is not described; the EU requirement calls for assessing adequacy, not just updating content.
Formal adherence assessment mechanisms and their causative analysis are not described; the EU requirement requires adherence evaluation and consideration of non-adherence causes.

synthesis_result.justification: Evidence shows periodic reassessment cadence, versioning with a changelog, and a living-document approach. Missing indicators are explicit event-driven assessment triggers, defined assessment scope/adequacy evaluation, formal adherence assessment, and remediation planning; their absence cannot be offset by periodic updates alone.

results.title: Risk identification process
results.requirement: Define a structured systemic risk identification process that is explicitly informed by the types of risks, the nature of systemic risks, and the sources of systemic risks as set out in Appendix 1, and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define a structured systemic risk identification process that is informed by the risk types (Appendix 1.1), the nature of systemic risks (Appendix 1.2), the sources of systemic risks (Appendix 1.3), and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks (Appendix 1.4)?
expected_evidence: The framework describes a structured process for identifying systemic risks stemming from the model.

The framework indicates that potential systemic risks are initially considered with reference to the types of risks defined in Appendix 1.1 (e.g. risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).

The framework explains that the identification process considers the nature of systemic risks, including essential and contributing characteristics such as scale, propagation, capability-dependence, or irreversibility (Appendix 1.2).

The framework describes how potential sources of systemic risks are considered in the identification process, including model capabilities, model propensities, and model affordances or contextual factors (Appendix 1.3).

The framework explicitly indicates that the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 are taken into account as part of the systemic risk identification process, such as risks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.
results.reasoning: The framework does not present a structured systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1.1–1.4. It shows governance/risk management functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and ongoing risk monitoring, but lacks an Appendix-aligned identification workflow and explicit inclusion of Appendix 1 risk types, nature, sources, or the specified systemic risks.
key_aligned_concepts: Governance structures and risk management functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)

results.title: Risk scenarios
results.requirement: The framework defines the need for the development of systemic risk scenarios for each identified systemic risk, including the appropriate number and level of detail of such scenarios.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define the need for the development of systemic risk scenarios for each identified systemic risk, including the appropriate number and level of detail of scenarios?
expected_evidence: The framework states that systemic risk scenarios are to be developed.
The framework states that systemic risk scenarios are developed for each identified systemic risk.
The framework indicates that the number of systemic risk scenarios should be appropriate.
The framework indicates that the level of detail of systemic risk scenarios should be appropriate.
results.reasoning: None of the four Expected Evidence indicators are evidenced in the retrieved material: (1) development of systemic risk scenarios, (2) development for each identified systemic risk, (3) appropriate number, and (4) appropriate level of detail. Gap analysis confirms the framework lacks operational requirements for systemic risk scenario development, so these indicators cannot be satisfied by thematic alignment alone.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: The framework does not define or require the development of systemic risk scenarios for identified systemic risks.
It does not specify the number of systemic risk scenarios that should be developed for each identified systemic risk.
It does not specify the level of detail appropriate for systemic risk scenarios.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The framework does not address the development of systemic risk scenarios for each identified systemic risk, including the appropriate number and level of detail of such scenarios.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: No substantive alignment: the text covers general AI risk management (GOV/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE) and risk tolerances but does not define systemic risk scenarios or their quantity/detail.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The retrieved framework does not define or require the development of systemic risk scenarios for identified systemic risks, nor specify the appropriate number or level of detail for such scenarios, leaving a gap relative to the EU requirement.
missing_elements: A requirement that systemic risk scenarios be developed for each identified systemic risk.
Specification that the number of systemic risk scenarios should be appropriate for each identified systemic risk.
Specification that the level of detail of systemic risk scenarios should be appropriate for each identified systemic risk.
weaker_areas: Overall framework emphasizes general risk management (GOV/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE) and risk tolerances but does not operationalize systemic risk scenario development.
scope_divergences: EU requirement explicitly mandates systemic risk scenario development for identified systemic risks with defined quantity and detail; the external framework lacks these elements and remains at a general risk management level.

synthesis_result.justification: None of the four Expected Evidence indicators are evidenced in the retrieved material: (1) development of systemic risk scenarios, (2) development for each identified systemic risk, (3) appropriate number, and (4) appropriate level of detail. Gap analysis confirms the framework lacks operational requirements for systemic risk scenario development, so these indicators cannot be satisfied by thematic alignment alone.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: The framework does not define or require the development of systemic risk scenarios for identified systemic risks.
It does not specify the number of systemic risk scenarios that should be developed for each identified systemic risk.
It does not specify the level of detail appropriate for systemic risk scenarios.

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to

selected_evidence.text:
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and
others. Priority research and additional guidance that will enhance this Framework will be
captured in an associated AI Risk Management Framework Roadmap to which NIST and
the broader community can contribute.

Framework will employ a two-number versioning system to track and identify major and minor changes. The
first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will
change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number
(e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including
version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook
frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time
and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.

results.title: Model-independent information
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the gathering of model-independent information relevant to systemic risk analysis, including how the breadth and depth of information gathering are determined in relation to the systemic risk.
results.assessment_question: Does the organisation systematically gather and document model-independent information relevant to identified systemic risks, using structured methods such as web searches or OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses of comparable models, training data reviews, historical incident analysis, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, and/or stakeholder or community engagement?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information.
The framework explains that the breadth and depth of model-independent information gathering are adjusted based on the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The framework indicates categories of methods that may be used to gather model-independent information, such as web searches or open-source intelligence, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews or panels, and participatory or community-based research methods.

The framework clarifies the role of model-independent information in informing subsequent stages of systemic risk analysis (e.g. evaluations, modelling, or estimation), without requiring that such stages have already been performed.
results.reasoning: Indicator 1 is supported by evidence showing model-independent contextual information informing risk analysis (expert consultation/external AI actors). Indicators 2, 3 (full catalog of methods), and 4 (clear articulation of informing subsequent stages without requiring those stages) are not fully satisfied; the text lacks explicit breadth/depth criteria, a complete methods catalog, and a clear mechanism linking model-independent information to later risk analysis stages independent of those stages being performed.
key_aligned_concepts: Model-independent contextual information informs systemic risk analysis (MAP/MEASURE)
Engagement with external AI actors and expert consultation as information gathering methods
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit breadth and depth adjustment criteria for model-independent information gathering, tied to the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

A complete, enumerated catalog of gathering methods (including web searches/OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews/panels, and participatory/community-based methods).

The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on
a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors
– established in GOVERN and carried out in MAP – is utilized in this function to decrease
the likelihood of system failures and negative impacts. Systematic documentation practices
established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.

and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems and to allocate risk management resources based on
assessed and prioritized risks. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply
the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or
expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

4.
Effectiveness of the AI RMF
Evaluations of AI RMF effectiveness – including ways to measure bottom-line improvements in the trustworthiness of AI systems – will be part of future NIST activities, in
conjunction with the AI community.
Organizations and other users of the Framework are encouraged to periodically evaluate
whether the AI RMF has improved their ability to manage AI risks, including but not limited to their policies, processes, practices, implementation plans, indicators, measurements,
and expected outcomes. NIST intends to work collaboratively with others to develop metrics, methodologies, and goals for evaluating the AI RMF’s effectiveness, and to broadly

of AI system risks and potential impacts to individuals, communities, organizations,
and society;

NIST AI 100-1

Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to
organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some
features in common with the AI RMF. Like most risk management approaches, they are
outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these
frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for
addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance
are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and

is acceptable to organizations or society are highly contextual and application and use-case
specific. Risk tolerances can be influenced by policies and norms established by AI system owners, organizations, industries, communities, or policy makers. Risk tolerances are
likely to change over time as AI systems, policies, and norms evolve. Different organizations may have varied risk tolerances due to their particular organizational priorities and
resource considerations.
Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may
be contexts where a risk management framework is not yet readily applicable for mitigating
negative AI risks.
The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices
which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations

first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will
change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number
(e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including
version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook
frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time
and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.

organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,

results.title: Post-market monitoring
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to systemic risk assessment and updating, and how independent external evaluators are intended to be enabled under appropriate safeguards, where applicable.
results.assessment_question: What post-market monitoring methods are required for assessing and mitigating systemic risk, and under what conditions and safeguards must independent external evaluators be granted access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced model variants, including protections against legal retaliation and responsible vulnerability disclosure timelines?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.
The framework explains that post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and decisions on framework or report updates.

The framework indicates that a range of post-market monitoring methods may be used, such as collecting end-user feedback, providing reporting or incident channels, engaging with affected stakeholders, monitoring public sources, or supporting independent research.
The framework describes how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.
The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

The framework explains the safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, and non-retaliation commitments.
results.reasoning: The text includes in-production post-market monitoring and ongoing risk tracking, but it fails to explicitly enumerate post-market monitoring methods, define access for external evaluators, describe safeguards, or clearly tie monitoring to systemic risk acceptability decisions and framework/report updates.
key_aligned_concepts: In-production monitoring (production TEVV) aligned with post-market monitoring
Regular risk tracking and updates to risk management
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit enumeration of post-market monitoring methods (e.g., end-user feedback collection, incident reporting channels, stakeholder engagement, monitoring public sources, and supporting independent research).
A clear mechanism showing how post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and triggers updates to the framework or its reports.
Clarification of applicability: how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.

Explicit conditions under which independent external evaluators are granted access to the model for post-market monitoring (including access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced variants).

Detailed safeguards for external evaluator access, including selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, non-retaliation commitments, and associated timelines/retention provisions.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text emphasizes in-production monitoring, TEVV-based measurement, and regular risk tracking to inform risk management, but does not specify concrete post-market monitoring methods nor explicit access conditions or safeguards for independent external evaluators to view model versions, chains-of-thought, or safety-reduced variants.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: It conceptually aligns with post-market monitoring through in-production monitoring and risk tracking, but lacks explicit operational requirements for external evaluator access and associated safeguards.

expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risk acceptance is determined for each identified systemic risk.
The framework defines systemic risk acceptance tiers or, where tiers are not suitable and the risk is not a specified systemic risk, alternative acceptance criteria.

Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may

negative AI risks.
The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices
which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations
should follow existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and
response established by organizational, domain, discipline, sector, or professional
requirements. Some sectors or industries may have established definitions of harm or
established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and

established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and
use case settings. Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should
define reasonable risk tolerance. Once tolerance is defined, this AI RMF can be used
to manage risks and to document risk management processes.
1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

results.title: Proceeding decisions
results.requirement: Describe how the framework defines decisions to proceed with, restrict, or not proceed with the development, making available on the market, or use of the model based on systemic risk acceptance determination.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how decisions to proceed or not proceed with the development, market availability, or use of the model are made based on systemic risk acceptance determination, and how responses are defined when risks are not acceptable or are likely to become unacceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework states that proceeding with development, making available on the market, or use of the model is conditional on systemic risks being determined acceptable.
The framework states that if systemic risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable, appropriate measures must be taken before proceeding.
The framework describes possible actions when risks are not acceptable, such as not making the model available on the market, restricting availability, withdrawing, or recalling the model.
The framework states that safety and/or security mitigations are to be implemented when systemic risks are not acceptable.

The framework states that another round of systemic risk identification, systemic risk analysis, and systemic risk acceptance determination is to be conducted when risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable.
results.reasoning: The text discusses risk tolerance and governance structures but provides no explicit decision gates or mandated actions to proceed/restrict/not proceed with development, market availability, or use based on systemic risk acceptance, nor any required mitigations or re-assessment triggers. None of the five indicators are explicitly addressed in an operational, binding manner.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The EU requirement calls for explicit decision gates to proceed, restrict, or not proceed with development/market use based on systemic risk acceptance, plus mandated mitigations and re-assessment when risks are unacceptable. The retrieved text provides high-level risk governance and risk tolerance concepts but lacks explicit, binding decision criteria, actions, mitigations, or re-assessment triggers tied to systemic risk acceptance.
missing_elements: Explicit decision points or gates to proceed with development, market availability, or use based on systemic risk acceptance determination.
Mandated actions when systemic risks are not acceptable (e.g., restrict, withdraw, recall, or prohibit market availability).
Requirement to implement safety and/or security mitigations as a condition to proceed when systemic risks are not acceptable.
Obligation to conduct another round of systemic risk identification, analysis, and acceptance determination if risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to become unacceptable.
weaker_areas: Presence of risk tolerance and governance structures is not binding or operationally specific enough to constitute explicit decision gates for proceeding with development/market use.
scope_divergences: Text centers on internal risk governance (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) rather than external, prescriptive obligations or regulatory decision rights to proceed/restrict/withdraw.
No explicit triggers, timelines, or retention requirements for re-assessment when systemic risks become unacceptable or are foreseeably about to become unacceptable.

synthesis_result.justification: The text discusses risk tolerance and governance structures but provides no explicit decision gates or mandated actions to proceed/restrict/not proceed with development, market availability, or use based on systemic risk acceptance, nor any required mitigations or re-assessment triggers. None of the five indicators are explicitly addressed in an operational, binding manner.

Governance structures (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) for AI risk management

No requirement to implement safety/security mitigations as a condition to proceed when systemic risks are not acceptable

1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

results.title: Safety mitigations
results.requirement: The framework defines and requires the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define and require the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework describes categories or types of safety mitigations intended to address systemic risks.
The framework explains that safety mitigations are designed to be robust under adversarial pressure, such as attempts to bypass or subvert them.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations take into account the model's release and distribution strategy.
The framework provides examples of safety mitigation approaches, such as e.g. input or output filtering, behaviour modification, staged access, or other emerging safety techniques.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations are considered and adapted across the model lifecycle.
results.reasoning: Indicators 1, 3, and 5 are supported by the text (lifecycle-focused mitigation categories, consideration during release/deployment, and lifecycle adaptation). Indicators 2 (robustness under adversarial pressure) and 4 (explicit examples of mitigation techniques) are not clearly established in the text, so they are not fully met; this cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone per the gap analysis.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle-based safety mitigations
Robustness/adversarial resilience
Deployment/guide for responsible use
Real-time monitoring and human intervention
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit operational mitigation techniques examples (e.g., input/output filtering, behavior modification, staged access) are not codified as requirements.
Explicit linkage and governance to the model’s release/distribution strategy with defined criteria or triggers are not substantively specified.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes, the text discusses lifecycle-focused safety considerations, robustness under varied conditions, and deployment-related information that align with implementing mitigations across the model lifecycle to address systemic risks, including intervention capabilities.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text demonstrates conceptual alignment with SS-5.1 by outlining lifecycle safety practices and robustness, plus deployment information; however, it remains high-level and does not provide explicit operational mitigations or detailed release-strategy requirements.

Deployment/guide for responsible use
Real-time monitoring and human intervention

operation of AI systems is improved through:
• responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
• clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;
• responsible decision-making by deployers and end users; and
• explanations and documentation of risks based on empirical evidence of incidents.
Different types of safety risks may require tailored AI risk management approaches based
on context and the severity of potential risks presented. Safety risks that pose a potential
risk of serious injury or death call for the most urgent prioritization and most thorough risk
management process.

Employing safety considerations during the lifecycle and starting as early as possible with
planning and design can prevent failures or conditions that can render a system dangerous.
Other practical approaches for AI safety often relate to rigorous simulation and in-domain
testing, real-time monitoring, and the ability to shut down, modify, or have human intervention into systems that deviate from intended or expected functionality.
AI safety risk management approaches should take cues from efforts and guidelines for
safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.

selected_evidence.text:
segments.
Robustness or generalizability is defined as the “ability of a system to maintain its level
of performance under a variety of circumstances” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Robustness is a goal for appropriate system functionality in a broad set of conditions and
circumstances, including uses of AI systems not initially anticipated. Robustness requires
not only that the system perform exactly as it does under expected uses, but also that it
should perform in ways that minimize potential harms to people if it is operating in an
unexpected setting.
Validity and reliability for deployed AI systems are often assessed by ongoing testing or
monitoring that confirms a system is performing as intended. Measurement of validity,
accuracy, robustness, and reliability contribute to trustworthiness and should take into consideration that certain types of failures can cause greater harm. AI risk management efforts
should prioritize the minimization of potential negative impacts, and may need to include
human intervention in cases where the AI system cannot detect or correct errors.
3.2
Safe
AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life,
health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe
operation of AI systems is improved through:
• responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
• clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;

safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.
3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

results.title: Security mitigations
results.requirement: The framework defines how security mitigations are selected and applied to meet the Security Goal, including alignment with the mitigation objectives set out in Appendix 4 or the use of equivalent alternative measures, and specifies that implementation may be staged across the model lifecycle as model capabilities increase.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how security mitigations are selected to meet the Security Goal, how the mitigation objectives defined in Appendix 4 (e.g. general security, protection of unreleased model parameters, interface hardening, insider threat protection, and security assurance) are addressed or achieved through equivalent measures, and how implementation is intended to be staged over the model lifecycle?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly links security mitigations to achieving a defined Security Goal.

The framework indicates that security mitigations align with the mitigation objectives defined in Appendix 4, such as general security protections, protection of unreleased model parameters, interface-access hardening, insider threat mitigation, and security assurance.

The framework indicates that specific security measures may vary depending on organisational context or infrastructure, and explains how alternative mitigations achieve equivalent mitigation objectives.
The framework indicates that security mitigations may be implemented in stages as model capabilities increase along the model lifecycle.
results.reasoning: Evidence shows lifecycle-stage governance (GOV/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE) and security evaluations, which partially address the criterion. However, there is no explicit linkage of security mitigations to a defined Security Goal, nor explicit alignment with Appendix 4 mitigation objectives (or equivalent), no described mechanism for selecting mitigations based on context, and no clear staged implementation plan tied to increasing model capabilities. These missing elements cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle-stage implementation of security measures (GOV/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE)

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

the effectiveness of testing and can mitigate internal biases and potential conflicts of interest.
Where tradeoffs among the trustworthy characteristics arise, measurement provides a traceable basis to inform management decisions. Options may include recalibration, impact
mitigation, or removal of the system from design, development, production, or use, as well
as a range of compensating, detective, deterrent, directive, and recovery controls.
After completing the MEASURE function, objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation,
verification, and validation (TEVV) processes including metrics, methods, and methodologies are in place, followed, and documented. Metrics and measurement methodologies
should adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms and be carried out in an open and transparent process. New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be
developed. The degree to which each measurement type provides unique and meaningful
information to the assessment of AI risks should be considered. Framework users will enhance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track
existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. Measurement outcomes will
be utilized in the MANAGE function to assist risk monitoring and response efforts. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems
as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

results.requirement: Describe, in the Model Report, the model’s characteristics and intended behaviour, including a high-level description of the model, its intended and actual uses, version differences, and a model specification explaining how the model is intended to operate.
results.assessment_question: Does the Model Report describe the model’s architecture, capabilities, propensities, and affordances, its intended and actual uses, differences between model versions, and its intended behaviour (including principles, refusal topics, and system prompt or references thereto)?
expected_evidence: The Model Report provides a high-level description of the model’s architecture, capabilities, propensities, and affordances, and how it differs from other models made available by the provider.
The Model Report describes how the model has been used and how it is intended to be used, including relevant use contexts.
The Model Report identifies model versions that are or will be made available on the market and explains relevant differences, including differences in systemic risks or mitigations.

The Model Report includes or references a model specification describing how the model is intended to operate, including guiding principles, prioritisation of instructions, refusal topics, and the system prompt (or a valid reference to it).

results.title: Reasons for proceeding
results.requirement: Describe how the Model Report explains the reasons for proceeding with the development, making available on the market, and/or use of the model, based on the systemic risk acceptance determination defined in the framework (including safety margins).
results.assessment_question: Does the Model Report explain the reasons for proceeding in a way that is consistent with the framework’s systemic risk acceptance determination, including safety margins, foreseeable undermining conditions, and the described decision-making process?
expected_evidence: The Model Report explains why the systemic risks are considered acceptable for this model, with reference to the acceptance logic and safety margins defined in the framework.
The Model Report identifies foreseeable conditions under which this justification would no longer hold.
The Model Report describes how the decision to proceed was made in line with the framework, including whether external actors or independent external evaluators informed the decision.
results.reasoning: The Model Report does not provide model-specific justification that systemic risks are acceptable with defined safety margins, nor does it identify foreseeable undermining conditions or document the decision-making process (including external evaluators). Indicators are therefore not met; only general risk tolerance and governance references are present.

The text also lacks any identification of foreseeable undermining conditions or a described decision-making process (including external evaluators) required by SS-7.2.

Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

results.requirement: Describe in the Model Report how the systemic risk framework has been applied to the model, including reported results of systemic risk identification, analysis, modelling, estimation, evaluations, implemented safety and security mitigations, their limitations, and planned future developments.
results.assessment_question: What must the Model Report document regarding systemic risk identification, modelling, and estimates, including model evaluation results with random input/output samples, comparisons between safety-mitigated and fully elicited model versions, independent external evaluator access, Security Goal and mitigation limitations, and planned future model capabilities over the next six months?
expected_evidence: The Model Report describes the reported results of systemic risk identification and analysis, including assumptions, uncertainties, and links to the risk types defined in the framework.
The Model Report explains the reported outcomes of systemic risk modelling and estimation, including how risks are characterised and compared with and without mitigations.
The Model Report summarises relevant model evaluation approaches and results used to understand systemic risks, including illustrative examples or references.
The Model Report describes implemented safety mitigations and their limitations, and explains how they align with the framework’s safety requirements.
The Model Report describes the Security Goal and implemented security mitigations, including alignment with defined mitigation objectives or justified alternatives.
The Model Report includes a high-level forward-looking description of planned model developments and anticipated changes to capabilities, risks, and mitigations.

results.title: Model report updates
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines obligations to update the Model Report when the justification for systemic risk acceptability is materially undermined, and whether it specifies periodic update expectations, versioning, and changelog requirements in line with Measure 7.6.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe when Model Report updates are required, including material undermining triggers, timing expectations, periodic updates for most capable models, and versioning/changelog requirements?
expected_evidence: The framework describes circumstances under which the justification for systemic risk acceptability may be materially undermined and requires a Model Report update in such cases.
The framework lists or references example triggers for updates, such as material changes in model capabilities, use, integrations, serious incidents, or evaluation validity.
The framework specifies expectations regarding the timing of Model Report updates, including completion within a reasonable time and prior to market release for deliberate changes.
The framework acknowledges periodic Model Report updates for the most capable models (e.g. at least every six months), including applicable exemptions.
The framework requires updated Model Reports to include versioning information and a changelog explaining how and why updates were made.
results.reasoning: No explicit Model Report update triggers, timing before market release, or periodic updates for the most capable models are present. While versioning and a changelog exist, they apply to the AI RMF Playbook rather than to Model Reports, and the indicators concerning Model Report-specific triggers, timing, cadence, and changelog are unmet.
key_aligned_concepts: Major/minor versioning with a changelog (Version Control Table)
Living document with periodic update cadence
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Indicator 1: No description of circumstances under which the justification for systemic risk acceptability may be materially undermined and require a Model Report update.
Indicator 2: No listing/reference of model-report-specific triggers for updates (e.g., changes in capabilities, use, integrations, incidents, evaluation validity).
Indicator 3: No timing expectations for Model Report updates, including completion within a reasonable time and prior to market release for deliberate changes.
Indicator 4: No acknowledgment of periodic Model Report updates for the most capable models (e.g., at least every six months) with exemptions.

Indicator 5: No requirement that updated Model Reports include versioning information and a changelog specific to Model Reports (current versioning/changelog described appears to target the AI RMF Playbook, not Model Reports).

• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and
