Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.

public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

results.title: AI Office notification
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework acknowledges the obligation to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and any updates, including timing requirements, permitted delays, interim reporting, and conditions for redactions in line with Measure 7.7.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe obligations to provide the AI Office with access to the Model Report and updates, including timing rules, permitted delays with interim reporting, and conditions for redactions?
expected_evidence: The framework states that the AI Office must be provided with access to the Model Report by the time a model is placed on the market.
The framework specifies that updates to the Model Report must be made accessible to the AI Office within a defined timeframe (e.g. five business days).
The framework acknowledges conditions under which redactions may be applied, such as requirements arising from national security laws.
The framework describes the possibility of delaying provision of the Model Report or updates for a limited period (e.g. up to 15 business days), subject to good-faith conditions.
The framework requires or acknowledges the provision of an interim Model Report containing specified information when such a delay is used.
The framework describes acceptable access mechanisms (e.g. publicly accessible link or secure channel specified by the AI Office).
results.reasoning: No indicators from the Expected Evidence set are present in the retrieved framework: (1) access to the Model Report by market placement, (2) defined timeframe for updates (e.g., five business days), (3) redaction conditions, (4) ability to delay up to 15 business days, (5) interim Model Report when delaying, (6) acceptable access mechanisms. Without these binary, actionable obligations, the framework cannot satisfy EU Measure 7.7, and thematic alignment cannot compensate for missing operational requirements.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No reference to providing AI Office access to the Model Report by market release
No defined timeframe for updates to the Model Report (e.g., five business days)
No acknowledgment of redaction conditions (e.g., under national security laws)
No provision for delaying the Model Report or updates up to 15 business days in good faith
No requirement to provide an interim Model Report containing specified information when a delay is used
No description of acceptable access mechanisms (e.g., publicly accessible link or secure channel)

results.title: Responsibilities
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines clear responsibilities for managing systemic risks, including systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance, and how these responsibilities are allocated across organisational governance levels.
results.assessment_question: How must signatories assign systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance responsibilities across the management body in its supervisory and executive functions, operational teams, and internal and external assurance providers, including role-specific requirements such as separation from core business activities and cascading responsibility structures for SMEs and SMCs?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly defines responsibilities for systemic risk oversight, ownership, support and monitoring, and assurance.
The framework describes how systemic risk oversight is assigned to a supervisory or otherwise independent governance function.
The framework describes how systemic risk ownership is assigned to executive-level functions responsible for risk-producing activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk support and monitoring is assigned to functions that are organisationally independent from core business activities.
The framework describes how systemic risk assurance is provided to a supervisory or independent body, including internal and, where applicable, external assurance.
The framework acknowledges proportional allocation of responsibilities based on organisational size and complexity (e.g. SMEs or SMCs).
results.reasoning: Found: indicator 3 (systemic risk ownership assigned to executive-level functions) is evidenced by GOVERN 2.3. Missing: indicators 2, 4, 5, and 6 (independent supervisory/assurance function, separation from core activities, internal/external assurance, and SME/SMC proportional tailoring) as well as explicit definitions of oversight/assurance responsibilities. The framework relies on cross-cutting governance rather than an explicit independent supervisory/assurance structure, and lacks SME/SMC-specific tailoring; thematic alignment cannot compensate for these operational gaps.
key_aligned_concepts: Executive leadership ownership of AI risk decisions
Documented roles, responsibilities, and lines of communication for AI risk management
Ongoing monitoring and periodic review of risk management processes
Resource allocation according to organizational risk priorities
AI risk management training for personnel and partners
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Absence of an independent supervisory or governance function for systemic risk oversight
No explicit systemic risk assurance mechanism (internal or external) to a supervisory or independent body
Lack of explicit separation from core business activities for governance and risk-management responsibilities
No explicit proportional tailoring of responsibilities for SMEs/SMCs

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text defines governance roles and responsibilities for AI risk management, including executive ownership of risk decisions, documented roles and lines of communication, and ongoing monitoring, aligning with several EU elements, but it does not explicitly describe independent supervisory/assurance structures or explicit proportional tailoring for SMEs/SMCs.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework aligns with the EU requirement on assigning systemic risk ownership and governance roles (executive ownership, documented responsibilities, and ongoing monitoring). It does not explicitly describe independent supervisory/assurance functions or explicit SME/SMC proportional tailoring.

GOVERN is a cross-cutting function that is infused throughout AI risk management and
enables the other functions of the process. Aspects of GOVERN, especially those related to
compliance or evaluation, should be integrated into each of the other functions. Attention
to governance is a continual and intrinsic requirement for effective AI risk management
over an AI system’s lifespan and the organization’s hierarchy.
Strong governance can drive and enhance internal practices and norms to facilitate organizational risk culture. Governing authorities can determine the overarching policies that
direct an organization’s mission, goals, values, culture, and risk tolerance. Senior leadership sets the tone for risk management within an organization, and with it, organizational
culture. Management aligns the technical aspects of AI risk management to policies and
operations. Documentation can enhance transparency, improve human review processes,
and bolster accountability in AI system teams.
After putting in place the structures, systems, processes, and teams described in the GOVERN function, organizations should benefit from a purpose-driven culture focused on risk

and documented.

Manage
The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on
a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors
– established in GOVERN and carried out in MAP – is utilized in this function to decrease
the likelihood of system failures and negative impacts. Systematic documentation practices
established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.
After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring
and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems and to allocate risk management resources based on
assessed and prioritized risks. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply
the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or
expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

results.title: Incident identification
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines methods and channels for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the model lifecycle, including consideration of external sources and facilitation of third-party reporting.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe approaches for identifying serious incidents, including monitoring external sources and enabling third-party reporting?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly recognises the need to identify and track serious incidents across the model lifecycle.
The framework describes intended methods for identifying serious incidents, including reference to post-market monitoring or similar processes.
The framework references consideration of external information sources (e.g. media, incident databases, research, public reporting).
The framework describes how downstream providers, users, or other third parties may report serious incidents to the Signatory and/or authorities.
results.reasoning: Found references to lifecycle governance (GOV/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE) and monitoring of third-party resources (MANAGE 3.1) and a risk-response mechanism (MANAGE 2.3). However, the text does not explicitly define methods to identify and track serious incidents across the lifecycle, lacks defined channels for third-party reporting to Signatories or authorities, contains no explicit post-market/incident monitoring linkage, and provides no explicit use of external information sources for incident identification. Therefore, operational indicators are missing and cannot be offset by thematic alignment.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle governance functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE
Monitoring of third-party resources (MANAGE 3.1)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit mechanisms to identify and track serious incidents across the AI model lifecycle (identification, logging, escalation, tracking).
Defined channels and processes for third-party reporting of serious incidents to Signatories and/or authorities.
Explicit post-market monitoring or equivalent processes tied to incident detection and lifecycle-tracking.
Explicit incorporation of external information sources (e.g., media, incident databases, research, public reporting) as inputs for incident identification.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The framework partially addresses the assessment question by incorporating lifecycle-wide governance and monitoring of third-party resources, but it does not explicitly define methods, channels, or processes for identifying, tracking, and reporting serious incidents, including external sources and third-party reporting.

results.title: Incident documentation
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines the information that should be tracked, documented, and reported for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, mitigation failures or circumvention, and handling of incomplete information.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, including root cause analysis and treatment of missing information?
expected_evidence: The framework defines the categories of information to be documented for serious incidents (e.g. timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
The framework specifies that a root cause analysis should be conducted, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
The framework describes how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring may inform incident analysis.
The framework acknowledges that some information may be unavailable at the time of reporting and requires such gaps to be explicitly recorded.
The framework indicates that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the severity of the incident.
results.reasoning: The framework currently does not define a minimum information set for serious incidents, nor a root cause analysis requirement, handling of missing information, or proportionality guidance for documentation. Retrieved evidence only shows post-deployment monitoring and incident communication without addressing the core operational indicators.
key_aligned_concepts: Post-deployment AI system monitoring
Incident tracking and communication to affected communities
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit minimum information categories for serious incidents (e.g., timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, response actions)
A defined root cause analysis requirement, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations
Mechanism showing how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring inform incident analysis
Explicit guidance that information may be incomplete at reporting time and must be explicitly recorded as gaps
Guidance that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the incident severity (including any thresholds or severity scales)

results.requirement: The framework defines mandatory severity-based reporting timelines for serious incidents involving the model, including differentiated deadlines for initial reports based on incident type, requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and submission of a final report after incident resolution.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify clearly differentiated reporting timelines for serious incidents (including specific deadlines for initial notification based on severity), periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and a final report after resolution?
expected_evidence: The framework defines categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
The framework associates specific deadlines for initial reporting following awareness of a serious incident (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days depending on severity).
The framework clarifies that reporting is triggered when the organisation becomes aware of the involvement of its model, including cases of reasonable suspicion of causal linkage.
The framework specifies periodic intermediate updates for unresolved serious incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks after the initial report).
The framework defines a deadline for submitting a final report after resolution of the serious incident (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).
The framework allows aggregation of multiple similar serious incidents within defined reporting timelines while respecting the earliest applicable deadline.

frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for

define reasonable risk tolerance. Once tolerance is defined, this AI RMF can be used
to manage risks and to document risk management processes.
1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

results.requirement: Define and maintain retention requirements ensuring that serious-incident documentation is preserved for at least five years from the later of the documentation date or the incident date.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define retention requirements for serious-incident documentation that meet or exceed a five-year period?
expected_evidence: The framework states that documentation of information related to serious incidents must be retained.
The framework specifies a minimum retention period of at least five years.
The framework indicates that the retention period is counted from the later of the documentation date or the date of the serious incident.
results.reasoning: None of the three Expected Evidence indicators are present in the retrieved text: (1) retention of serious-incident documentation, (2) a minimum five-year retention period, and (3) counting the retention period from the later of the documentation date or incident date. As these are operational retention requirements, their absence cannot be offset by thematic alignment to governance/framework versioning.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing retention requirement for serious-incident documentation.
Missing minimum five-year retention period for serious-incident documentation.
Missing definition of how retention is calculated (counting from the later of the documentation date or incident date).

alignment_findings.alignment_summary: There is no alignment. The retrieved text discusses framework versioning and governance but does not address retention of serious-incident documentation.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The retrieved text does not define or specify retention requirements for serious-incident documentation, including a five-year minimum and the counting rule. It focuses on versioning and governance, not regulatory incident-retention obligations.

scope_divergences: Focus on framework versioning/governance rather than regulatory retention obligations for serious incidents; no retention-related content is present, indicating a divergence from the EU requirement.

results.requirement: Define and maintain additional detailed documentation describing the model’s architecture, integration into AI systems, evaluation approaches and results, and implemented safety mitigations, and ensure such documentation can be provided to the AI Office upon request and is retained for at least ten years after market placement. The framework should also define how key systemic risk decisions and justifications are documented.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define requirements to maintain, retain, and make available additional detailed documentation and decision justifications for AI Office review?
expected_evidence: Documentation defines requirements for maintaining detailed model architecture descriptions.
Documentation defines requirements for describing model integration into AI systems (where applicable).
Documentation defines requirements for documenting model evaluations, results, and evaluation strategies.
Documentation defines requirements for documenting implemented safety mitigations.
Documentation defines how key systemic risk processes, decisions, and justifications are recorded.
Documentation specifies retention periods for additional documentation (e.g. at least 10 years).
results.reasoning: None of the six Expected Evidence indicators are demonstrated in the retrieved text; the framework only shows high-level governance and versioning of risk-management content but lacks explicit, operational requirements (e.g., model architecture documentation, integration, evaluation details, safety mitigations, decision justifications, and a ten-year retention with external AI Office access), so the EU Code of Practice requirements are not satisfied.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit requirement to maintain detailed documentation describing the model’s architecture.
Explicit requirement to document integration of the model into AI systems (where applicable).
Explicit requirement to document evaluation approaches and results, and evaluation strategies.
Explicit requirement to document implemented safety mitigations.
Explicit requirement to document key systemic risk processes, decisions, and justifications.
Retention period requirement of at least ten years after market placement for the documentation.
Mechanism to provide the documentation to the AI Office upon request.
Clear alignment or mapping of these documentation requirements to the EU Code of Practice specifics.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No; the framework discusses governance and versioning of AI risk management content but does not define explicit requirements to maintain, retain for a defined period, or make available additional detailed documentation and decision justifications for AI Office review.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The document shows general documentation governance (versioning and change history) but lacks explicit, operational requirements mapped to the EU Code of Practice's retention, content, and external access aspects.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The framework lacks explicit, binding requirements to maintain, retain for a defined period (ten years), and make available detailed documentation and decision justifications for AI Office review. It only references high-level governance and versioning of AI risk management content, not content-specific documentation or external reporting obligations.

results.title: Public transparency
results.requirement: Define when and how summarised public versions of the Framework and Model Reports are published for the purpose of systemic risk assessment and mitigation, including safeguards to protect sensitive information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations. The framework should also define conditions under which public publication is not required (e.g. similarly safe or safer models).
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define conditions, scope, safeguards, and exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports?
expected_evidence: The framework states that summarised versions of the Framework and Model Reports may be published.
The framework indicates that publication is required when necessary for systemic risk assessment or mitigation.
The framework indicates that removals or redactions are applied to protect sensitive commercial information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.
The framework states that Model Report summaries include high-level descriptions of systemic risk assessment results and safety and security mitigations.
The framework defines exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.
results.reasoning: All indicators are missing; the retrieved text does not address publishing public summaries or any conditions, safeguards, or exceptions for such publication. The gap analysis identifies missing elements including publication conditions, redaction mechanisms, content requirements for Model Report summaries, and explicit publication exceptions.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Definition of conditions, scope, safeguards, and exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports.
Statement that summarised versions may be published and the circumstances that trigger publication for systemic risk assessment or mitigation.
Mechanisms for removals or redactions to protect sensitive commercial information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.
Content requirements for Model Report summaries, including high-level descriptions of systemic risk assessment results and mitigations.
Defined exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The retrieved text does not define conditions, scope, safeguards, or exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: No alignment with the EU requirement on publishing public summaries is observable; the text discusses AI risk management framework structure without publication-specific conditions or safeguards.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The retrieved text does not address publishing public summaries of the Framework or Model Reports, nor any conditions, safeguards, or exceptions for such publication. There is no mention of redactions, content of summaries, or publication triggers for systemic risk assessment.
missing_elements: Definition of conditions, scope, safeguards, and exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports.
Statement that summarised versions may be published and the circumstances that trigger publication for systemic risk assessment or mitigation.
Mechanisms for removals or redactions to protect sensitive commercial information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.
Content requirements for Model Report summaries, including high-level descriptions of systemic risk assessment results and mitigations.
Defined exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.
scope_divergences: Publication policy is absent; the text focuses on internal risk management functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and does not specify external disclosure requirements.

synthesis_result.justification: All indicators are missing; the retrieved text does not address publishing public summaries or any conditions, safeguards, or exceptions for such publication. The gap analysis identifies missing elements including publication conditions, redaction mechanisms, content requirements for Model Report summaries, and explicit publication exceptions.

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to
organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some
features in common with the AI RMF. Like most risk management approaches, they are
outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these
frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for
addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance
are unable to:
• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;
• account for the complex attack surface of AI systems or other security abuses enabled
by AI systems; and

criteria.title: Create a Safety & Security Framework
criteria.requirement: Define a state-of-the-art Safety and Security Framework that conceptually describes how systemic risks are assessed, accepted, and mitigated across the model lifecycle.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define, at a conceptual and descriptive level, the key elements required for systemic risk management under the Safety and Security Chapter (including trigger points, risk acceptance logic, mitigation expectations, responsibility allocation, external input, and update processes)?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly describes its purpose as managing systemic risks associated with general-purpose AI models.
The framework outlines how systemic risks are identified, assessed, and mitigated at a high level.
The framework describes trigger points at which additional evaluations or assessments would occur during the model lifecycle.
The framework defines how systemic risk acceptability is determined, including the use of risk tiers or acceptance criteria.
The framework describes, at a high level, expected categories or types of safety and security mitigations associated with different risk levels.
The framework explains how responsibility for systemic risk assessment and mitigation is allocated within the organization.
The framework describes whether and how input from external actors may influence risk-related decisions.
The framework describes how and under what conditions the framework itself would be reviewed or updated.

criteria.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework is intended to be applied across the entire model lifecycle, including continuous systemic risk assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident inputs, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how its systemic risk assessment and mitigation processes are intended to be applied across the model lifecycle, including continuous assessment activities, trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, incident consideration, and escalation to a full systemic risk assessment?
expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risks are continuously assessed along the entire model lifecycle.
The framework explains how lighter-touch evaluations are conducted at predefined trigger points (e.g. based on time, development stage, compute, access, or affordances).
The framework describes how post-market monitoring is conducted to inform ongoing systemic risk assessment.
The framework explains how information about serious incidents or near misses is taken into account within the risk assessment process.

The framework describes how results from trigger-point evaluations, post-market monitoring, or incident inputs can lead to deeper analysis or escalation to a full systemic risk assessment and mitigation process.

Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.

negative risk can mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the integrity of the decision process.

Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.
Page 24
NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
This complexity and varying levels of visibility can introduce uncertainty into risk management practices. Anticipating, assessing, and otherwise addressing potential sources of
negative risk can mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the integrity of the decision process.

system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.

criteria.title: Framework updates
criteria.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework defines the conditions, processes, and scope for periodic and event-driven framework assessments and updates, including versioning, changelogs, and remediation planning, in line with Measure 1.3 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define how and when framework assessments and updates are intended to occur, including assessment triggers, periodic review, evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, and the handling of remediation and versioning?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that it is subject to periodic reassessment (e.g. at defined intervals) and to reassessment when specified conditions or events occur.

The framework describes conditions or triggers that would lead to a framework assessment (e.g. material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
The framework explains the scope of a framework assessment, including the evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
The framework explains that framework adherence is assessed, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
The framework describes how findings from a framework assessment may lead to updates of the framework to keep it state-of-the-art.
The framework describes that updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog explaining the nature and rationale of changes.
The framework describes how remediation plans are intended to be defined when framework assessments identify risks of continued or future non-adherence.
criteria.reasoning: Evidence shows periodic reassessment cadence, versioning with a changelog, and a living-document approach. Missing indicators are explicit event-driven assessment triggers, defined assessment scope/adequacy evaluation, formal adherence assessment, and remediation planning; their absence cannot be offset by periodic updates alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Periodic reassessment at defined intervals (semi-annual)
Versioning with a changelog
Living document with ongoing updates and stakeholder feedback
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit event-driven assessment triggers (conditions or events that would trigger a framework assessment)
Defined scope of a framework assessment, including evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to systemic risks
Formal mechanism for assessing framework adherence, including how non-adherence is identified and its causes
Remediation planning processes to address risks from assessments and how remediation findings lead to updates

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text partially addresses SS-1.3 by detailing periodic assessments/updates, versioning with a changelog, and ongoing ‘living document’ updates, but it does not explicitly define event-driven assessment triggers, the assessment scope, adherence evaluation, or remediation planning.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework establishes periodic review, versioning, and ongoing updates, but it lacks explicit event-triggered assessment triggers, adherence evaluation scope, and remediation planning.
key_aligned_concepts: Periodic reassessment at defined intervals (semi-annual)
Versioning with a changelog
Living document with ongoing updates and stakeholder feedback

evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Indicator: Periodic reassessment/defined intervals (operational).

evidence_citations.quote: Be a living document. The AI RMF should be readily updated as technology, understanding, and approaches to AI trustworthiness and uses of AI change and as stakeholders learn from implementing AI risk management generally and this framework in particular.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Articulates the expectation that the framework evolves with changing understanding and practice.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Indicator: Updates keep framework state-of-the-art (conceptual/operational).

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The framework covers periodic reassessment and versioning with a living document, but it omits explicit event-driven assessment triggers, explicit assessment scope/adequacy evaluation, adherence assessment, and remediation planning.
missing_elements: Explicit event-driven assessment triggers (conditions or events that would trigger a framework assessment, such as material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, or materially changed systemic risks).
Defined scope of a framework assessment, including explicit evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to systemic risks of the AI models.
Formal mechanism for assessing framework adherence, including how non-adherence is identified and its causes analyzed.
Remediation planning processes to address risks from assessments, including how remediation findings lead to framework updates and responsibilities for remediation actions.
weaker_areas: Adherence evaluation—the text does not define the scope or method for assessing adherence to the framework.
Assessment scope and adequacy evaluation—no explicit description of what the framework assessment should examine beyond periodic updates.
scope_divergences: Lacks explicit event-driven assessment triggers; the EU requirement calls for conditions/events that trigger assessments, not only periodic reviews.
Remediation planning is not described; the EU requirement expects remediation planning when risks of non-adherence are identified.
Explicit evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to systemic risks is not described; the EU requirement calls for assessing adequacy, not just updating content.
Formal adherence assessment mechanisms and their causative analysis are not described; the EU requirement requires adherence evaluation and consideration of non-adherence causes.

criteria.title: Risk identification process
criteria.requirement: Define a structured systemic risk identification process that is explicitly informed by the types of risks, the nature of systemic risks, and the sources of systemic risks as set out in Appendix 1, and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define a structured systemic risk identification process that is informed by the risk types (Appendix 1.1), the nature of systemic risks (Appendix 1.2), the sources of systemic risks (Appendix 1.3), and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks (Appendix 1.4)?
expected_evidence: The framework describes a structured process for identifying systemic risks stemming from the model.

The framework indicates that potential systemic risks are initially considered with reference to the types of risks defined in Appendix 1.1 (e.g. risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).

The framework explains that the identification process considers the nature of systemic risks, including essential and contributing characteristics such as scale, propagation, capability-dependence, or irreversibility (Appendix 1.2).

The framework describes how potential sources of systemic risks are considered in the identification process, including model capabilities, model propensities, and model affordances or contextual factors (Appendix 1.3).

The framework explicitly indicates that the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 are taken into account as part of the systemic risk identification process, such as risks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.
criteria.reasoning: The framework does not present a structured systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1.1–1.4. It shows governance/risk management functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and ongoing risk monitoring, but lacks an Appendix-aligned identification workflow and explicit inclusion of Appendix 1 risk types, nature, sources, or the specified systemic risks.
key_aligned_concepts: Governance structures and risk management functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Risk framing and ongoing monitoring
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No defined, formalized systemic risk identification process informed by Appendix 1.1–1.4,
No explicit integration of Appendix 1.1 risk types, Appendix 1.2 risk characteristics, Appendix 1.3 sources, or Appendix 1.4 specified systemic risks in the identification process
No documented roles, inputs, outputs, or frequency/timing for systemic risk identification

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No—the AI RMF framework outlines governance, mapping, measuring, and managing risk and risk framing, but it does not define a structured systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1.1–1.4.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework provides general risk framing and governance structures that align with risk management concepts, but it lacks an explicit, structured systemic risk identification process tied to Appendix 1 risk types, sources, and specified systemic risks.
key_aligned_concepts: Governance structures and risk management functions (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)

evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Shows cross-framework alignment but does not provide explicit systemic risk identification steps.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The EU requires a clearly defined, Appendix 1–informed structured systemic risk identification process; the framework provided relies on general governance/risk management constructs without an explicit, Appendix-aligned systemic risk identification workflow.
missing_elements: A defined, formalized systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1.1–1.4 (types, nature, and sources of systemic risks).
Explicit integration of Appendix 1.1 risk types (e.g., risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society) into the systemic risk identification process.
Explicit integration of Appendix 1.2 characteristics of systemic risks (scale, propagation, capability-dependence, irreversibility) into the identification process.
Explicit integration of Appendix 1.3 sources of systemic risks (model capabilities, model propensities, model affordances, contextual factors) into the identification process.

Explicit inclusion of Appendix 1.4 specified systemic risks (e.g., CBRN threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offense, harmful manipulation) within the systemic risk identification process.
Documented roles, inputs, outputs, and frequency/timing for performing systemic risk identification within the organization.
weaker_areas: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE provide general risk management, governance, and ongoing monitoring but do not establish a binding, Appendix-1–based systemic risk identification mechanism.
Asset inventory and risk prioritization activities are present but not oriented toward a systematic identification of systemic risks as defined in Appendix 1.
scope_divergences: Divergence in approach: EU requirement expects Appendix 1–based systemic risk identification; the framework presents generic risk management functions without tying identification to Appendix 1 risk types/sources/nature.
Divergence in content: The framework does not reference Appendix 1 risk types, nature, sources, or the specified systemic risks in its identification process.

Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may

negative AI risks.
The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices
which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations
should follow existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and
response established by organizational, domain, discipline, sector, or professional
requirements. Some sectors or industries may have established definitions of harm or
established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and

may consider leveraging available standards and guidance that provide broad guidance to
organizations to reduce security and privacy risks, such as, but not limited to, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the NIST Privacy Framework, the NIST Risk Management Framework, and the Secure Software Development Framework. These frameworks have some
features in common with the AI RMF. Like most risk management approaches, they are
outcome-based rather than prescriptive and are often structured around a Core set of functions, categories, and subcategories. While there are significant differences between these
frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for
addressing many other types of risks – frameworks like those mentioned above may inform
security and privacy considerations in the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions of the
AI RMF.
At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance

• adequately manage the problem of harmful bias in AI systems;
• confront the challenging risks related to generative AI;
• comprehensively address security concerns related to evasion, model extraction, membership inference, availability, or other machine learning attacks;

selected_evidence.text:
Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and
others. Priority research and additional guidance that will enhance this Framework will be
captured in an associated AI Risk Management Framework Roadmap to which NIST and
the broader community can contribute.

Framework will employ a two-number versioning system to track and identify major and minor changes. The
first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will
change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using “.n” after the generation number
(e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including
version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook
frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time
and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.

criteria.title: Model-independent information
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the gathering of model-independent information relevant to systemic risk analysis, including how the breadth and depth of information gathering are determined in relation to the systemic risk.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the organisation systematically gather and document model-independent information relevant to identified systemic risks, using structured methods such as web searches or OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses of comparable models, training data reviews, historical incident analysis, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, and/or stakeholder or community engagement?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information.
The framework explains that the breadth and depth of model-independent information gathering are adjusted based on the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The framework indicates categories of methods that may be used to gather model-independent information, such as web searches or open-source intelligence, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews or panels, and participatory or community-based research methods.

The framework clarifies the role of model-independent information in informing subsequent stages of systemic risk analysis (e.g. evaluations, modelling, or estimation), without requiring that such stages have already been performed.
criteria.reasoning: Indicator 1 is supported by evidence showing model-independent contextual information informing risk analysis (expert consultation/external AI actors). Indicators 2, 3 (full catalog of methods), and 4 (clear articulation of informing subsequent stages without requiring those stages) are not fully satisfied; the text lacks explicit breadth/depth criteria, a complete methods catalog, and a clear mechanism linking model-independent information to later risk analysis stages independent of those stages being performed.
key_aligned_concepts: Model-independent contextual information informs systemic risk analysis (MAP/MEASURE)
Engagement with external AI actors and expert consultation as information gathering methods
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit breadth and depth adjustment criteria for model-independent information gathering, tied to the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

A complete, enumerated catalog of gathering methods (including web searches/OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews/panels, and participatory/community-based methods).

missing_elements: Explicit breadth and depth adjustment criteria for model-independent information gathering, tied to the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The EU requirement emphasizes model-independent information informing later risk analysis stages without requiring those stages to be performed; the text does not clearly establish this sequential independence.

The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on
a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors
– established in GOVERN and carried out in MAP – is utilized in this function to decrease
the likelihood of system failures and negative impacts. Systematic documentation practices
established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.
After completing the MANAGE function, plans for prioritizing risk and regular monitoring
and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems and to allocate risk management resources based on
assessed and prioritized risks. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply
the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or
expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

The MANAGE function entails allocating risk resources to mapped and measured risks on
a regular basis and as defined by the GOVERN function. Risk treatment comprises plans to
respond to, recover from, and communicate about incidents or events.
Contextual information gleaned from expert consultation and input from relevant AI actors
– established in GOVERN and carried out in MAP – is utilized in this function to decrease
the likelihood of system failures and negative impacts. Systematic documentation practices
established in GOVERN and utilized in MAP and MEASURE bolster AI risk management
efforts and increase transparency and accountability. Processes for assessing emergent risks
are in place, along with mechanisms for continual improvement.

and improvement will be in place. Framework users will have enhanced capacity to manage the risks of deployed AI systems and to allocate risk management resources based on
assessed and prioritized risks. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue to apply
the MANAGE function to deployed AI systems as methods, contexts, risks, and needs or
expectations from relevant AI actors evolve over time.

4.
Effectiveness of the AI RMF
Evaluations of AI RMF effectiveness – including ways to measure bottom-line improvements in the trustworthiness of AI systems – will be part of future NIST activities, in

whether the AI RMF has improved their ability to manage AI risks, including but not limited to their policies, processes, practices, implementation plans, indicators, measurements,

Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,

positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.

Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability

result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the

occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.

expected_evidence: The framework describes that probability and severity of harm are estimated as part of systemic risk analysis.

is acceptable to organizations or society are highly contextual and application and use-case
specific. Risk tolerances can be influenced by policies and norms established by AI system owners, organizations, industries, communities, or policy makers. Risk tolerances are

resource considerations.
Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may
be contexts where a risk management framework is not yet readily applicable for mitigating
negative AI risks.
The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices
which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations

version number, date of change, and description of change. NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook
frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time

criteria.title: Post-market monitoring
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to systemic risk assessment and updating, and how independent external evaluators are intended to be enabled under appropriate safeguards, where applicable.
criteria.assessment_question: What post-market monitoring methods are required for assessing and mitigating systemic risk, and under what conditions and safeguards must independent external evaluators be granted access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced model variants, including protections against legal retaliation and responsible vulnerability disclosure timelines?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.
The framework explains that post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and decisions on framework or report updates.

The framework indicates that a range of post-market monitoring methods may be used, such as collecting end-user feedback, providing reporting or incident channels, engaging with affected stakeholders, monitoring public sources, or supporting independent research.
The framework describes how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.
The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

The framework explains the safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, and non-retaliation commitments.
criteria.reasoning: The text includes in-production post-market monitoring and ongoing risk tracking, but it fails to explicitly enumerate post-market monitoring methods, define access for external evaluators, describe safeguards, or clearly tie monitoring to systemic risk acceptability decisions and framework/report updates.
key_aligned_concepts: In-production monitoring (production TEVV) aligned with post-market monitoring
Regular risk tracking and updates to risk management
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit enumeration of post-market monitoring methods (e.g., end-user feedback collection, incident reporting channels, stakeholder engagement, monitoring public sources, and supporting independent research).
A clear mechanism showing how post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and triggers updates to the framework or its reports.
Clarification of applicability: how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.

Explicit conditions under which independent external evaluators are granted access to the model for post-market monitoring (including access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced variants).

Detailed safeguards for external evaluator access, including selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, non-retaliation commitments, and associated timelines/retention provisions.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text emphasizes in-production monitoring, TEVV-based measurement, and regular risk tracking to inform risk management, but does not specify concrete post-market monitoring methods nor explicit access conditions or safeguards for independent external evaluators to view model versions, chains-of-thought, or safety-reduced variants.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: It conceptually aligns with post-market monitoring through in-production monitoring and risk tracking, but lacks explicit operational requirements for external evaluator access and associated safeguards.

evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Directly references monitoring of the AI system during production, a core aspect of post-market monitoring.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: MEASURE 2.4 in-production monitoring (post-market monitoring).

evidence_citations.quote: MEASURE 2.6: The AI system is evaluated regularly for safety risks – as identified in the MAP function. Safety metrics reflect system reliability and robustness, real-time monitoring, and response times for AI system failures.

evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Regular evaluation for safety risks and real-time monitoring.

New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be developed. Framework users will enhance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may

The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices
which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations
should follow existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and
response established by organizational, domain, discipline, sector, or professional
requirements. Some sectors or industries may have established definitions of harm or
established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and

use case settings. Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should
define reasonable risk tolerance. Once tolerance is defined, this AI RMF can be used
to manage risks and to document risk management processes.
1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

criteria.title: Proceeding decisions
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines decisions to proceed with, restrict, or not proceed with the development, making available on the market, or use of the model based on systemic risk acceptance determination.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how decisions to proceed or not proceed with the development, market availability, or use of the model are made based on systemic risk acceptance determination, and how responses are defined when risks are not acceptable or are likely to become unacceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework states that proceeding with development, making available on the market, or use of the model is conditional on systemic risks being determined acceptable.
The framework states that if systemic risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable, appropriate measures must be taken before proceeding.
The framework describes possible actions when risks are not acceptable, such as not making the model available on the market, restricting availability, withdrawing, or recalling the model.
The framework states that safety and/or security mitigations are to be implemented when systemic risks are not acceptable.

The framework states that another round of systemic risk identification, systemic risk analysis, and systemic risk acceptance determination is to be conducted when risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable.
criteria.reasoning: The text discusses risk tolerance and governance structures but provides no explicit decision gates or mandated actions to proceed/restrict/not proceed with development, market availability, or use based on systemic risk acceptance, nor any required mitigations or re-assessment triggers. None of the five indicators are explicitly addressed in an operational, binding manner.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The EU requirement calls for explicit decision gates to proceed, restrict, or not proceed with development/market use based on systemic risk acceptance, plus mandated mitigations and re-assessment when risks are unacceptable. The retrieved text provides high-level risk governance and risk tolerance concepts but lacks explicit, binding decision criteria, actions, mitigations, or re-assessment triggers tied to systemic risk acceptance.
missing_elements: Explicit decision points or gates to proceed with development, market availability, or use based on systemic risk acceptance determination.
Mandated actions when systemic risks are not acceptable (e.g., restrict, withdraw, recall, or prohibit market availability).
Requirement to implement safety and/or security mitigations as a condition to proceed when systemic risks are not acceptable.
Obligation to conduct another round of systemic risk identification, analysis, and acceptance determination if risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to become unacceptable.
weaker_areas: Presence of risk tolerance and governance structures is not binding or operationally specific enough to constitute explicit decision gates for proceeding with development/market use.
scope_divergences: Text centers on internal risk governance (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) rather than external, prescriptive obligations or regulatory decision rights to proceed/restrict/withdraw.
No explicit triggers, timelines, or retention requirements for re-assessment when systemic risks become unacceptable or are foreseeably about to become unacceptable.

Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

criteria.title: Safety mitigations
criteria.requirement: The framework defines and requires the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define and require the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework describes categories or types of safety mitigations intended to address systemic risks.
The framework explains that safety mitigations are designed to be robust under adversarial pressure, such as attempts to bypass or subvert them.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations take into account the model's release and distribution strategy.
The framework provides examples of safety mitigation approaches, such as e.g. input or output filtering, behaviour modification, staged access, or other emerging safety techniques.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations are considered and adapted across the model lifecycle.
criteria.reasoning: Indicators 1, 3, and 5 are supported by the text (lifecycle-focused mitigation categories, consideration during release/deployment, and lifecycle adaptation). Indicators 2 (robustness under adversarial pressure) and 4 (explicit examples of mitigation techniques) are not clearly established in the text, so they are not fully met; this cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone per the gap analysis.

Real-time monitoring and human intervention

Robustness or generalizability is defined as the “ability of a system to maintain its level
of performance under a variety of circumstances” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Robustness is a goal for appropriate system functionality in a broad set of conditions and
circumstances, including uses of AI systems not initially anticipated. Robustness requires
not only that the system perform exactly as it does under expected uses, but also that it
should perform in ways that minimize potential harms to people if it is operating in an
unexpected setting.
Validity and reliability for deployed AI systems are often assessed by ongoing testing or
monitoring that confirms a system is performing as intended. Measurement of validity,
accuracy, robustness, and reliability contribute to trustworthiness and should take into consideration that certain types of failures can cause greater harm. AI risk management efforts
should prioritize the minimization of potential negative impacts, and may need to include
human intervention in cases where the AI system cannot detect or correct errors.

operation of AI systems is improved through:

safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.
3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.
